notes.meaning: Jesus finished teaching His great sermon to the listening crowd and entered the town of Capernaum. This bustling fishing town served as His main home base during His public ministry. He returned there to continue His work among the people.

A Roman army officer known as a centurion had a servant who was dying from a severe illness. A centurion commanded about one hundred soldiers in the Roman military. Roman law allowed masters to mistreat or abandon sick slaves, but this officer cared deeply for his servant.

When the officer heard that Jesus had arrived, he sent some respected Jewish leaders to ask Him for help. As a Gentile outsider, the officer felt unworthy to approach a Jewish teacher directly. He asked these leaders to plead with Jesus to come and heal his dying servant.
The Jewish leaders came to Jesus and pleaded urgently for the Roman officer. They told Jesus that the man truly deserved His help. They believed his good deeds made him worthy of a miracle.

The leaders explained that the officer loved the Jewish people and had paid to build their local synagogue. A synagogue was a Jewish building used for prayer and studying Scripture. It was rare for a Roman officer to show such generosity and honor to the God of Israel.

Jesus agreed and started walking toward the officer's home. Before He reached the house, the officer sent friends with a message asking Jesus not to trouble Himself. The centurion explained that he was not worthy to have Jesus enter his home, knowing that entering a Gentile house could make a Jewish teacher ritually unclean.

The officer felt so unworthy that he had not dared to meet Jesus face to face. He asked Jesus simply to speak a word of command from where He stood so his servant would recover. He believed Jesus had full power over sickness even from a distance.

The officer explained his faith by pointing to his own military life. He was under the orders of higher commanders, and soldiers and servants obeyed his commands instantly when he spoke. He realized that Jesus held the same kind of absolute authority over disease and nature.

Jesus was amazed by what the officer had said. He turned to the crowd following Him and said He had not found such great faith even among the people of Israel. A foreign soldier trusted the Lord more boldly than many who had grown up learning God's laws.

The friends returned to the officer's home and found the dying servant completely healed. Jesus had healed him instantly without ever stepping foot inside the house. His spoken word carried all the power needed to restore the man.
Soon afterward, Jesus traveled to a small town called Nain. His disciples and a large crowd went along with Him. Nain was a village in Galilee situated south of Mount Tabor.

As Jesus reached the town gate, He met a funeral procession carrying a dead young man out for burial. He was the only son of a widowed mother, leaving her without family or financial support. A large crowd from the town was walking with her to mourn the terrible loss.
When the Lord saw the weeping mother, His heart went out to her with deep compassion. He told her not to weep. He stepped in to help her out of pure mercy before anyone had even asked.

Jesus walked up and touched the open funeral stretcher, causing the pallbearers to stop. Touching a funeral bed normally made a person ceremonially unclean under Jewish law, but Jesus brought life instead of defilement. He then commanded the dead young man to get up.
The dead young man sat up right away and began to speak. His speech proved that he was fully alive and well. Jesus then gently gave the young man back to his mother.

A deep sense of awe swept over everyone in the crowd, and they praised God. They said that a great prophet had risen among them and that God had come to help His people. Raising the dead brought to mind the mighty works of the ancient prophets Elijah and Elisha.
The news of this resurrection spread far and wide through Judea and all the surrounding country. People everywhere began talking about Jesus' miraculous power over death.

Disciples of John the Baptist visited him and told him about all these miracles. King Herod had locked John in a fortress prison, but his followers were still allowed to visit him. They kept him informed about Jesus' growing ministry.

John called two of his disciples and sent them to ask Jesus if He was the promised Messiah or if they should look for someone else. The phrase 'the One who was to come' was a recognized title for the Messiah. Older commentators noted that John asked this so his disciples could see Jesus for themselves and settle their own doubts.

differ.view: John did not doubt for himself, but sent his disciples so their doubts would be settled by seeing Jesus firsthand.
John himself was wrestling with doubt in prison because Jesus was not bringing the swift political deliverance he had expected.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars teach that John himself was struggling with doubt while suffering in prison, wondering why Jesus had not yet overthrown their enemies.

notes.meaning: The two messengers reached Jesus and repeated John's exact question. They asked whether Jesus was indeed the promised Deliverer or if they needed to wait for someone else. They wanted a clear answer from Jesus' own lips.

At that very moment, Jesus healed many people of diseases, painful afflictions, and evil spirits, and He restored sight to the blind. Rather than just offering words, He let John's messengers see His divine power with their own eyes.

Jesus told the messengers to return to John and report what they had seen and heard. The blind could see, the lame could walk, lepers were cured, the deaf could hear, the dead were raised, and the poor heard the good news of salvation. These exact miracles fulfilled the ancient prophecies of Isaiah about the Messiah.

Jesus declared that anyone who does not lose faith on account of Him is truly blessed. Many people expected the Messiah to be an earthly general who would overthrow Rome, so Jesus warned them not to stumble over His humble work of mercy.

Once John's messengers departed, Jesus began speaking to the crowds about John. He asked if they had gone out to the desert to see a reed swaying in the breeze, which pictured a weak man who shifts with public opinion. Jesus affirmed that John was not fickle, but strong and steady in his witness.

Jesus asked if they had gone into the wilderness to see someone dressed in fancy, luxurious clothing. People who wear fine robes and enjoy soft living reside in royal palaces, not dry deserts. John was a rugged, self-denying prophet who lived simply to deliver God's call to repentance.
